The session begins.

The Trade Way ends in noise. Carts grind onto the stones of Wyrm's Crossing, porters shout over each other, and somewhere above the river a bell marks the evening. Lamps are being lit one by one along the bridge. Houses and shopfronts lean over the span, so the crossing feels less like a road and more like a narrow, crowded street hanging over the Chionthar.

The queue at the checkpoint shuffles forward. A family with bundles on their backs passes the trestle table; a carter argues about a toll and loses. Behind the table, a Flaming Fist sergeant with ink on her fingers and a chipped red gauntlet rubs her eyes and writes on a chalkboard without looking up much.

A few paces off the line, a lean man in a too-good waistcoat has turned a barrel into a table. Three cards flick under his hands, face down, face up, face down. "Find the lady, friends, find the lady! Long road, short game, a silver says you've still got your eye!" A couple of waiting drovers lean in to watch. The cards slap down again, crisp and familiar.

At James's feet, the cat has stopped. Its tail is up and its ears are turned, not toward the cards, but somewhere along the bridge, where the lamplight thins between two shuttered stalls.

The man in front of James steps up to the table. The sergeant's chalk taps the board.

"Next after this one — name, and your business in the Gate."

The sergeant doesn't look up until he gives the name. Then she does, briefly: at the faded regimental cloak first, then at his face. The chalk scratches.

"Worgen." She spells it under her breath and gets it right the first time. "Zaranda's. Long way from Tethyr." She writes a short word after the name, possibly *work*. "The Fist takes men. Seatower, mornings, ask for the recruiting clerk. Don't come drunk, they'll keep you." The chalk taps once. "Beds. On the bridge they're cheap and damp. Inside the wall they're dearer and dry. The Basilisk Gate shuts late, but not *that* late."

Her board is crowded: tonight's names in neat columns, older ones half-smeared at the edges. Beside a handful of the faded names there's a small chalk cross, very carefully drawn. The newest one has been gone over twice.

Ilse sees where he's looking and turns the board a little toward herself. She doesn't make a show of it.

"Foot's free. Carts pay." Her eyes go to the card game beside the queue for a moment, then come back to him. "You'll want to keep walking, Worgen."

---

The cat answers him the way it always does: in pictures and feelings, not words.

*Man.* Between the two shuttered stalls, back against the planks, where the lamplight doesn't reach. *Still. Not hiding hard. Just still.* *Eyes on the barrel.* The card-man's hands moving, the cards going down, a drover's silver crossing the barrel. *Lips moving every time money moves.*

Then something closer, from right under the barrel: a sour, cold smell, like a cellar where the water never quite dries out, with a trace of old candle smoke. The cat's fur rises along its spine. *That. Don't like that.*

The cat stays at his heel with its tail fluffed and its eyes on the dark between the stalls. Behind him the queue shuffles forward. Ahead the bridge runs on under the lamps toward the walls of the Lower City.

Ilse's chalk stops. She doesn't look at the barrel, and she doesn't look between the stalls either. She keeps her eyes on the board, like any sergeant checking a name.

"The one in the dark is Guild. Or he's running for them." She says it flatly, the way you'd mention the weather. "They send someone to count any table that doesn't pay them their share. If he's counting, Penhallow isn't paying. That's between the two of them."

Behind James a drover clears his throat loudly. Ilse ignores him.

"The game." She rolls the chalk once between ink-stained fingers. "Officially it's three cards and a man with quick hands. The Fist doesn't close card tables on this bridge. If we did, there'd be nobody left on it." Her thumb rests for a moment on the edge of the board, just beside the column he saw earlier, then moves away.

Then she looks up at him properly for the first time. She looks at the cat, then back at him.

"Foul how?"

Then she turns the board back toward him, only a little, just enough that he can see the crossed names under the lamp.

"Seven since spring." She keeps her voice level, the same flat tone as before. "I write them in when they come over the bridge. Some weeks later the harbour gives them back. Copper coin in the mouth. My captain says that's Umberlee taking her toll and not the Fist's business." She taps a cross with one ink-stained finger. "Harl Venn. Came up from Elturel with his mother, six weeks ago. Pulled out under the Rock the night before last."

The drover behind James sighs loudly enough for half the queue to hear. Ilse doesn't look round.

"I remember faces. It's most of the job. Five of the seven, I saw them stand at a table on this bridge. Some at his barrel. Some at the dice by the fish stalls. More than once." Her finger comes off the board. "That isn't proof. Half the bridge stands at a table sometime. But it's five out of seven."

She pulls the board back square in front of her and picks up the chalk.

"The ledgers are in the hut behind me. Every name since the winter, with the dates. I'm on till the late bell." She looks past his shoulder at the drover. "Next."

The cat doesn't move from his boot. Its ears are still turned toward the barrel, where Penhallow is fanning the three cards for a new mark and laughing at something nobody else heard.

"Late bell," Ilse says. She doesn't look up, and the drover behind James is already pushing up to the trestle.

James drifts out of the line and stops a little short of the barrel, at the edge of the small crowd. It's close enough to see the cards, and far enough back that nobody would take him for a player. The cat slips off his boot and drifts sideways along the planks like any bridge cat on its evening round.

Penhallow never stops talking. "There she is, friend, there's the lady, red as a bishop's blush. Watch her now, watch her go." A drover with a sunburnt neck puts down a silver. The cards move. For anyone who has dealt the throw a thousand times, there's nothing to it. Penhallow's right hand seems to drop its top card first, but it lets go of the bottom one. The queen stays pinched against his fingers for a heartbeat and goes down on the left, where the drover isn't looking. It's a good, clean hype, better than most on the southern coast. The drover points to the middle card and turns up a black jack. His silver goes into Penhallow's waistcoat pocket, and his friends laugh at him.

Next comes a boy, twelve or thirteen, all elbows, with the flat vowels of Elturel. He has a silver bit he holds like it's hot. This time Penhallow throws slowly, almost lazily. The queen goes exactly where any eye would follow it. The boy finds her. The crowd groans happily.

Penhallow doesn't pay the boy from the waistcoat pocket where the silver went. His left hand drops under the barrel's rim, and it comes back up with a fistful of coppers that he counts into the boy's palm: ten, along with the silver bit back. "Luck of the road, friend. Don't spend it all at once." The boy grins and is off north into the crowd before anyone can talk him into a second go.

Between the stalls, the still man's lips move.

---

The cat answers him from low down by the barrel's foot, in pictures:

*Dark inside. The barrel is hollow, open at the bottom.* There's a nail on the inside of a stave with a leather bag hanging from it, its mouth tied loose. *The smell is there. Strong.* Wet stone, old wax, and underneath it something the cat has no picture for. Its fur rises at it. *Too strong.* It backs off, as he told it to.

Then it shows him one more thing on its way out: a single copper on the planks just inside the rim, where a coin might fall from a hand counting too fast. *Same smell. Smaller.*

The cat comes back to sit behind James's heel, facing the barrel, tail thick.

---

Penhallow fans the three cards again, and this time his eyes find James over the heads of the drovers. They go to his hands first, then to the shut purse, and back up to his face. He smiles like a man who knows exactly what he's looking at.

"You've been watching my hands, friend, not my lady. That's a dealer's habit." The cards flick and settle and flick again. "One silver. Just to see if you're as good as you think you are?"

Dov's hands never stop. "Retired, friend? From cards?" He laughs and the three cards fan and close again. "Nobody retires. They just go quiet a while." He's already turned back to the drovers, but his eyes follow James out of the crowd for a step or two longer than a barker's would.

The boy hasn't gone far. The crush on the bridge thickens past the checkpoint: porters with poles across their shoulders, a woman with a basket of eels, a handcart with a wheel that squeals. James keeps the boy's elbows in sight without shoving anyone. The cat flows along at his heel, keeping clear of boots.

At James's call the boy stops and turns, fast, with his back to a lamp-post and his right fist shut tight against his chest. Up close he's thinner than he looked at the barrel. One bootlace has snapped and been knotted twice, and the knot has come loose again. There's a fresh scrape across the knuckles of his free hand, still beaded, the sort you get from a fall onto planks.

He looks at James, then at the cloak, then down at the cat. The cat looks back at him, and its tail, which has been fluffed since the barrel, doesn't settle.

"Wren says I'm not to talk to men who follow me." The Elturel vowels are flat and careful. He doesn't run, though. His eyes go to the cat again. "...Is that yours?"

He shifts his weight. The fist stays shut.

"Four times. Maybe five." Pride creeps in over the wariness. "I've got the eye. He says so himself, says I'm the only one on the bridge who can follow his lady. Harl told me about the table, back when we came over. He said it was the easiest money on the whole crossing." His mouth closes on the name, and for a moment he looks younger than twelve. "Harl's... he's not about anymore."

Behind him a carter yells and the handcart's wheel squeals past. The boy flinches at the noise more than he should, then frowns at James.

"What d'you want to know for, mister?"

The boy stays where he is with his back to the lamp-post. He doesn't run, though the room James leaves him to do it is plain enough. When James says *drowned*, the boy's shoulders jerk as if someone had slammed a shutter behind him. He looks at the cat rather than at James.

"He's not about," he says again, flatly, as if that settles it.

Then the question reaches him, and he frowns. He's a boy deciding whether any of it counts as strange.

"No dreams." He shrugs. "Nobody asks about my coppers. Nobody'd *think* to, I'm not worth robbing." He lifts his left hand and shows the scraped knuckles like a joke on himself. "Just stupid stuff. I fell on the planks this morning, nothing there, I just went down. The lace went twice. A dog had me by the coat on Rivington steps yesterday, and it's never bothered anyone before." He hesitates. He frowns harder, as if he's only now hearing it all laid end to end.

"That's just luck, though, mister. Everybody has—"

"*Pim.*"

She comes through the crush the way people do when they've been searching for a while, quick and sideways, one shoulder first. She's maybe seventeen and wiry, with a sleeve rolled to the elbow and a gutting apron still tied on under a shawl. The smell of the fish stalls comes with her. Her hair is tied back hard, and she has the same flat vowels as the boy.

She doesn't shout at him. She steps in between, close, and moves Pim behind her with one hand on his chest, not roughly. Then she looks at James properly: the old cloak, the rod at his belt, the soft boots, the hands. Last of all she looks at the cat.

Through the bond, the cat gives him a brief impression of her: *fish, river, sweat, tired.* Then it adds, with something like relief: *Not that smell. Not on her.* Its tail is still thick, and its ears are on the fist behind her back.

"I heard you from the stalls." Wren keeps her voice down. It isn't a voice for a crowd. "Asking him about his coppers. And about Harl."

She doesn't let go of her brother.

"Harl came down from Elturel in the same cart as us. He started winning at that barrel in the summer. Then it was his laces, then his hand in a door, then a cart wheel over his foot. He laughed about it. Said a man that lucky at cards was bound to pay somewhere." Her jaw sets. "Then the river. And now Pim's got the eye, Dov says, and Pim's falling over nothing on dry planks."

Behind her, Pim says "*Wren*," embarrassed. She doesn't look round.

"So you tell me, James with the cat. What do *you* know about that table?"

Wren listens to all of it without moving her hand off her brother's chest. When James says *separate bag*, her eyes narrow. When he says the cat reacts to Pim's winnings but not to her, she looks down at the cat, which is still staring at the boy's fist, tail still thick.

She doesn't answer about the sergeant. She looks at the scrap of cloth on his open palm, then at his face, and decides.

"Show him."

"Wren—"

"No bet, he said. Not buying. You heard him." She keeps her voice low and level. "Show him, Pim."

Pim's jaw works. He holds his shut fist up over the cloth for a long moment, like he's waiting for someone to grab it. Nobody does. Finally he turns his hand over and lets the coins slide out between his fingers without opening it all the way, and they land on the cloth in a little clatter. Ten coppers. The silver bit stays in his fist. He pulls his hand straight back against his chest.

The lamp on the post above them is good enough to see by. They're ordinary coppers at first glance: worn thin, mixed mints, one with a Tethyrian crown rubbed almost smooth, one clipped. Then James tips the cloth toward the light, and the edges catch it.

There's a mark on every one of them, on the rim and not the face, where nobody looks. It's tiny, smaller than a grain of rice: a branching shape pressed into the copper, not scratched, and dark, as if it had been burned in. A little antler.

He doesn't need a sage to tell him what it is. Every gambler on the southern coast knows that sign, and he has spent a lot of nights at tables with men who spat over their shoulder when someone said her name. Black antlers belong to Beshaba, the Maid of Misfortune, Tymora's sister and the other face of luck. He's seen the antler scratched on a loser's door, carved into a bandit's shield to frighten caravan guards, and drawn on the bottom of a bad dealer's cup as a joke. He has never seen it hidden on the rim of a coin, where only someone who knew to look would find it.

The coins are warm through the cloth, which is natural enough after the boy's fist. But the cloth is cool, and the warmth doesn't seem to be fading.

At his boot the cat has gone flat, with its ears back. Through the bond comes the same picture as at the barrel: *wet stone, old wax, the thing underneath.* Then, sharp: *On the cloth now. On you, close.* It doesn't come any nearer.

Wren has leaned in to look, and she sees the marks too. She doesn't know them, and James can tell from the way she squints. But she sees there are ten of them, one on every coin.

"That's on all of them." She straightens up. "Then he throws them in the river. Tonight."

"*No.*" Pim says it loud enough that a porter glances round. Then he drops his voice, but he doesn't back down. "I won them, Wren. Fair. That's two days' bread, mister. I've got the eye. They're *mine*."

Wren doesn't argue with him. She's looking at James.

"What's that on the edge?"

Wren goes very still at the name. She doesn't spit or make a sign. She just looks at the tiny dark antler for a long moment, and her jaw tightens.

"He *said* I had the eye." It comes out quiet. "Every time. He said only me." He shifts his weight, and his chin comes up anyway. "But I found her. You said. I found her proper."

"Pim eats." She says it like a rule she's just made. "I pay you back when the stalls pay me. That's how it is, or it's nothing."

The walk back is only a few dozen feet against the flow of the crowd. They pass the barrel on the way. Dov is fanning the cards for a carter's boy, and his patter doesn't stop. But his eyes come up and find them: James with a bundle in his hand, the Elturel boy and the fish-girl beside him, all of them heading for the Fist's trestle. The cards hang in his fingers half a beat longer than they should. Then he laughs and throws.

Ilse is arguing a toll with a man who has two goats and no money. She lets him go, goats and all, when she sees who's coming.

James opens the cloth on the trestle, below the lamp and out of sight of the queue. Ilse doesn't touch the coins either. She bends close, then closer, and finds the mark on the third coin. Once she's seen it, she finds it on the rest quickly.

"His barrel." It isn't a question. She looks at Pim and his bootlace, then at Wren. "Yours?"

"My brother," Wren says.

Ilse straightens up. She rolls the chalk once between her fingers, then puts it down.

"Harl Venn's coin went to my captain's desk with the report. They all do. I never looked at the edge." She keeps her voice flat. "I'll be looking now."

Then she answers the other question, the way she gives directions to the queue.

"Tymora. The Lady's Hall is up the hill, behind the inner wall. The Upper City gates shut at dark, and the Watch won't open them for anyone on this bridge without a patriar's seal." She stops, and something comes back to her. "One of theirs came down here, though. Three weeks back, maybe four. A grey-haired priestess in the Hall's blue, with a little counting-board on a string. She stood by my queue half a morning asking people when they'd last made an offering to the Lady, and whether their prayers had been answered. Odd questions. Sister Aurenna, she called herself." Ilse's eyes go back to the coins. "I took her for a temple collecting money. Maybe she wasn't."

Behind them the queue is getting longer. Ilse looks past James at it, then at the hut.

"Ledgers are in there, if you want them. It's quiet enough now."

"Wrapped. Not spent. Not swapped for others." He counts the conditions off as he goes. "And I'm where they are, mister. Till the priest. Then they come back to me, the same ten."

Ilse has dealt with two more carts while they talked. She waves the next one past without looking at it.

"She left nothing with me. No lodging, no name to ask for. She went back up the hill before the gates shut, I'd guess." She stops for a moment. "She didn't spend the whole day at my queue, though. In the afternoon she walked up to the Rock. There's a niche for the Lady at the foot of the chapel stair, where carters drop a copper before the road south. An old man sells candles there and minds the box. She was there a long while. I saw her go up, and I saw her come down near dark."

She looks at the queue, then at the hut behind her, then at James.

"The Rock's halfway across. The candle-man packs up when the lamps are all lit, more or less." Her eyes go back to the board. "Ledgers are still there. Coll goes to the fish stalls now."

She lifts two fingers. Coll stops picking at his thumb, sees her, and walks off slowly toward the smell of fish, the way a man walks when he's been told to look as if he isn't going anywhere.

The walk to the Rock takes them north against the evening traffic. They pass the shuttered stalls and the smell of the fish stalls. Coll is there now, leaning on a post with his arms folded, looking at a tray of eels as if he's thinking of buying one. Then the bridge widens and climbs. Wyrm's Rock rises out of the river in the middle of the crossing, black and wet at its foot. The fortress sits on top, and the roadway bends around its flank under the lamps.

Pim walks on the side away from the bundle, between his sister and the cat. He doesn't say anything. Twice his loose bootlace catches on a plank seam, and twice Wren takes hold of his collar before he can fall.

The chapel stair starts where the road bends: worn steps cut straight into the rock, climbing toward a door with a lamp above it. At the foot of the steps, set into the stone at about chest height, is the Lady's niche. It holds a weathered relief of a woman's face on a coin, worn smooth by hands, and in front of it a ledge of guttering candle-ends. There's an iron-bound box with a slot in the lid, chained to a ring in the rock.

Wren goes straight to the wall on their side of the blanket, kneels, and works a knife-tip under a short board. It comes up without a sound, as if it has done this often. Under it is a grey wool stocking knotted at the top. She lifts it out by the knot and doesn't open it. Then, under James's eyes, she does open it, just enough to tip a few coins into the rushlight on her palm.

The mark is on the rim of every one. They're the same little dark antlers.

She pours the coins back and counts the rest by touch through the wool, her lips moving. She stops and frowns.

"Thirty." She looks at Pim. "Four lots. That's forty."

Pim has gone red to the ears again. He keeps his voice down, for the sleeping children.

"First lot went through my coat. There was a hole in the pocket, I didn't know. On the bridge, by the Rock." He shoves his hand into the pocket and shows them his fingers poking out the bottom; nobody has mended it. "I thought that was the bad luck. Losing it straight off. Before you started keeping them."

Wren closes her eyes for half a breath. Then she knots the stocking shut, puts the board back, and stands up.

"Same as the river, then," she says to James, low. It isn't a question. Then she says to her brother, not unkindly, "Hole gets sewn tomorrow."

She goes out past Nell's mending with the stocking held away from her body, as James held the bundle.

---

Going down the stair, Pim keeps hold of the rail with both hands.

At the bottom Wren stops in the lane and answers what James said by the fire. She has clearly turned it over on the way.

"Ilse." She says the name like a price she doesn't like. "You tell her the silver and the coppers. She'll hear it from you. From a fish-girl she'd hear it and forget it." She shifts the stocking to her other hand. "If she asks me is it true, I'll say yes. To her face. That much I'll do."

The window of the Stave and Hoop glows a few yards on. Sentry trots ahead to the door and waits there, looking back at the stocking.

*Two lots now,* it tells him. *Both on the boy.* Its tail stays thick until they're inside.

The bar won't go across for a while yet. The fire's still up, and you can do what you like with the rest of the evening.

It has a narrow bed with a blanket folded at its foot, one shelf over the bed, one by the door and a horn window gone yellow with smoke. Sentry walks the length of the room once, inspects every snoring carter, and settles against the backs of his knees.

Sentry's head is up. Through the bond: *Up. The boy's room. Something fell.* A pause while it listens. *Girl awake. Quiet now.* Its head goes back down, but one ear stays turned toward the stair until James stops feeling it.

I turn away from the cards before my eyes can follow the lady, and step up to the sergeant.

“James Worgen. Formerly Queen Zaranda’s infantry. Looking for a bed tonight and honest work tomorrow.”

Keeping an eye on the cat, I ask it silently through our bond: *What have you spotted?*

I lean closer to the table and lower my voice so it won’t carry to the barrel.

“Before I go, Sergeant—there’s a man between those shuttered stalls watching the game. His lips move whenever money changes hands. My cat’s caught something foul under the barrel, too. Might be nothing, but is that game trouble you already know about?”

“Damp cellar. Old candle smoke. Enough to put its fur up.” I glance down at the cat. “Not proof of anything. But I’ve learned to listen when it dislikes something.”

I keep my voice low. “Those crosses beside the names—do they have anything to do with Penhallow’s table?”

“I’ll be back before the late bell,” I tell Ilse, and step out of the queue.

I drift toward the barrel, stopping where I can watch without joining the betting. Through the bond, I ask the cat: *Stay clear of hands and feet. Can you look beneath it from the side? Don’t touch anything—and back away if that smell gets stronger.*

While it looks below, I watch Penhallow’s hands and listen to his patter, leaving my purse firmly shut.

“Retired,” I say, with a smile that takes a little effort. “Keep your silver.”

I leave the barrel and follow the boy north, walking briskly without pushing through anyone. When I’m close enough to speak without shouting, I call, “Lad—a moment. I’m not after your winnings. Have you played at that table before?”

I stop a few paces away, leaving him room to go.

“Yes, the cat’s with me. And Wren’s given you sensible advice.” I lower my voice. “I’m James. The checkpoint sergeant told me Harl was found drowned. I’m sorry.”

“I don’t know what happened to him, but something about that table worries me. Has anything strange happened since you started winning—bad dreams, someone following you, anyone asking about your coppers?”

“Dov cheats the grown men. I watched him deliberately let Pim win, then pay him from a separate bag. My familiar caught a foul smell on that bag—and it’s reacting to Pim’s winnings now, but not to you.”

I keep my voice low. “That’s what I know. I suspect the coins, but I can’t yet tell you what’s wrong with them or how to put it right.”

I take out a clean scrap of cloth and spread it on my open palm.

“Pim, would you put the winnings here so I can examine them? No wager, and I’m not buying them off you. Then, if you’re willing, we should speak to Sergeant Ilse together. She’s noticed the drownings too.”

“Beshaba’s antlers. The Maid of Misfortune.” I show Wren one marked rim without touching the copper. “Hidden on every coin. This is no ordinary crooked game.”

I look at Pim. “You followed the lady correctly. But Dov chose what he paid you with. That part wasn’t fair.”

Keeping the cloth open, I add, “Don’t throw them in the river yet. We don’t know whether that would help. I’ll buy you both supper regardless of what happens to these—not payment for them, and not a trade.”

I nod back toward the checkpoint. “Let’s show Ilse these marks and ask where we can find a priest of Tymora tonight. I serve the Lady, but breaking curses needs more than a confident guess.”

“Dov saw us coming here. If those coins connect him to seven deaths, he may not stay at his barrel much longer.” I keep my voice below the noise of the queue. “Can you have someone keep him in sight? No confrontation yet.”

I fold the cloth shut and turn to Pim and Wren. “They’re still yours. Will you let me carry them wrapped until we find a priest? I don’t know whether keeping them off your skin helps, but the cat dislikes them just as much now.”

Then I ask Ilse, “Did Sister Aurenna leave word where she was staying outside the Upper City—or how to reach her?”

“Wrapped, not spent, not swapped. The same ten,” I agree. “And you stay with me.”

I nod to Ilse. “Thank you. We’ll try the candle-man before he leaves.”

With Pim, Wren and the cat, I head straight for the Lady’s niche at Wyrm’s Rock. If the candle-seller is still there, I approach with my coin of Tymora visible.

“Good evening. I’m looking for Sister Aurenna. Sergeant Ilse said she spoke with you a few weeks ago. A boy may be in danger—do you know how we can reach her tonight?”

I take two coppers from my own purse, keeping Pim’s bundle separate.

“Two candles, please.” I offer one to Pim. “For Harl, if you’d like. No need to say anything.”

I light mine at a burning stub and set it before the Lady’s face.

“Lady, you sent me here. Help me keep this boy safe until morning.”

Then I turn to Wren. “We should get that lace tied before we walk farther. Supper next, and I’ll be here for Aurenna after the morning bell. Do you have somewhere safe to sleep tonight?”

“Hadn’t got that far,” I admit. “A dry bed was the plan. It’s acquired complications.”

I glance at the wrapped coins. “I won’t ask you to take a stranger into your room. Let’s get those pies, then find an inn nearby with a common room where we can sit together. I’ll pay for beds if you’re comfortable staying. No debt for those—this investigation is my choice.”

I look at Pim. “You keep sight of your ten coppers, and nobody has to walk alone after dark.”

I thank Tobin for the cord and head with Wren and Pim toward the pie-woman’s stall.

“Three, please.” I pay six coppers from my own purse and hand Wren and Pim a pie each.

“That’s useful, Wren. Thank you. Tomorrow I’d like to hear exactly which way he goes.”

With the coins kept wrapped and separate, I take the steps carefully beside them toward the Stave and Hoop. Through the bond I ask the cat, *Watch behind us. Let me know if anyone keeps following when we turn.*

“The room with a door, please—for these two, if that suits them. And a long-room bed for me. We’ll sit together by the fire awhile first.”

I set six silver on the trestle, keeping Pim’s wrapped coins separate.

“Could you wake me before the first boats arrive? I’ve an early start.”

I offer Pim my untouched pie. “Here. I’d rather have a bowl of something hot.”

Through the bond, I tell the cat: *Leave the pie on the steps. You’ve earned supper that hasn’t fallen down a staircase.*

“You’re right, Pim. I said it, and I haven’t forgotten. They go upstairs with you when you’re ready for bed. I’m only carrying them until then.”

I turn to Wren. “Keep them wrapped and away from the bed, if you can. That’s a precaution, not a cure. I’ll come up before I go anywhere in the morning—we need to agree what happens next, not leave you guessing.”

I put two coppers on the trestle. “Pottage, please, Hessa. And have you a clean scrap of meat for the cat? I’ll pay for that too.”

Then I settle with Wren and Pim near the fire, the wrapped coins in sight. “Wren, when Dov comes back up those steps with his bag full, does he come alone?”

“Hasn’t told me,” I admit, watching it wash. “I’ve been waiting for an introduction. It seems to think feeding it is more urgent.”

Through the bond I ask, *Pim wants to know your name. So do I. Is there something you’d like us to call you?*

I turn back to Wren. “Thank you. What you’ve seen gives me somewhere to start. I’ll speak with you here before I leave in the morning—before you need to reach the stalls.”

“Sentry,” I say, looking at the cat. “First to notice trouble, first to inspect supper. Seems to fit.”

Through the bond I offer the name as a question, with a feeling of affection.

Then I finish my pottage and lean toward the wrapped coins without opening the cloth. Before I send Pim upstairs with them, I try to recall what I’ve learned of Beshaba’s curses: whether marked coins must remain in someone’s possession to work, and whether simply returning them could put anyone else at risk.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

“Wren. Pim.” I keep my voice quiet. “I’ve remembered something important. In the accounts I know, the curse follows ownership, not whoever’s holding the coins. Wrapping them won’t protect you, Pim. Nor would throwing them away. Spending them could pass the harm to someone else.”

I pause. “The same accounts say a cursed stake can go back to whoever placed it, through the same sort of bargain. But these coins are unusual. I want Aurenna’s advice before we try anything—and I’m not sending you back to Dov’s table.”

I look between them. “For tonight, we keep them safe and unspent. Tomorrow I’ll look for where Dov gets his bag filled, then meet the priestess. Have either of you seen him lose and pay someone from anywhere besides that bag?”

“You were being careful, Wren. Keeping him from spending them may have spared someone else.”

I glance toward the door. “We ought to collect the earlier winnings before someone at home finds them. All of us together, if you’re willing—Pim stays with his ten, as promised. Then straight back here.”

I keep my voice low. “Tomorrow, Ilse needs to hear what you’ve just told me: silver from his pocket for the drovers, marked coppers for folk nobody’s likely to look for. That’s deliberate choosing, not ordinary cheating.”

I pick up the wrapped bundle and wait for their agreement before heading for the cooperage.

“I’ll tell Ilse, and give you credit for noticing it,” I tell Wren. “You won’t have to start from nothing.”

I turn to Pim. “The lost ten matter too. We’ll tell Aurenna about them. Don’t go searching the bridge in the dark.”

Back inside, I accompany them upstairs and put the wrapped ten on the shelf by the door, beside the stocking, with Pim watching.

“Forty here. Ten lost. None spent. Have I got that right?”

Once we’ve checked, I bid them goodnight. “I’ll knock before I leave tomorrow. If anything happens tonight, wake me—third bed from the long-room door.”

I head down to that bed, keeping my gear close, and settle with Sentry nearby to sleep until Hessa’s early call.

The strongest part was how naturally the investigation grew out of arriving in the city. I had no quest, but the cards tempted James, the cat noticed something wrong, and Ilse gave me enough reason to get involved without hiring me. That felt well matched to this character.

**What worked**
- Wren and Pim felt like people rather than information dispensers. Pim’s pride in “having the eye,” his insistence on keeping his own coins, and Wren negotiating how she could repay help made the stakes personal.
- Sentry was excellent: useful sensory impressions, clear limits, and enough personality that naming the cat became a genuinely enjoyable moment.
- The clues developed coherently: separate payout bag, marked rims, selective victims, earlier winnings, then Dov’s morning supply trip. My questions and decisions seemed to uncover the story rather than merely advance a script.
- The Religion check was worthwhile. Its answer changed what I could responsibly do with the coins. Not rolling for straightforward conversations also kept play moving.

**What broke or dragged**
- Too many responses restated my entire turn, sometimes nearly line for line, before supplying the next development. That slowed otherwise good scenes.
- The repeated out-of-game explanations that honest conversation needed no roll were unnecessary. Just resolving those actions was enough.
- Timekeeping became inconsistent. Around quarter past nine, the late bell was still ahead; after further activity, I somehow completed eight hours’ rest before the first boats and morning bell. The schedule mattered because I was planning to intercept Dov.
- A “debt” for Wren’s pies appeared despite my offering supper freely. Wren can certainly *feel* indebted, but the journal should distinguish her intention from an obligation James accepted.

**What was missing**
- A little more actionable geography and timing: how long to reach the bridge from the inn, roughly when Dov usually passes, and how that relates to Aurenna’s arrival.
- More pressure or change outside our conversations. Coll watching Dov was promising, but much of the evening became a sequence of discussions and arrangements. One concrete update from that surveillance could have kept the wider world present.
- A clearer opportunity to respond to the nighttime thump. It was narrated inside the sleep-to-morning transition, which made a potentially important danger feel unavailable for intervention.

Overall, I cared about keeping these two safe, enjoyed playing James’s restraint around cards, and finished with a plan I wanted to pursue. Keep the characterful dialogue and clue logic; trim repetition and make the clock dependable.

Yes—the thump from Pim and Wren’s room during the night. I wanted to get up, knock quietly, and check that neither of them was hurt. We already knew Pim’s misfortune was escalating, so “something fell” wasn’t a sound James would comfortably ignore.

But that event and Hessa waking me in the morning arrived in the same response. By the time I could act, the night had passed and the long rest was complete. I felt I’d missed the chance rather than chosen to stay in bed.

Stopping at Sentry’s warning would have given me a meaningful decision: investigate and risk interrupting my rest, or trust Wren to handle it.

turns.reply:
The sergeant doesn't look up until he gives the name. Then she does, briefly: at the faded regimental cloak first, then at his face. The chalk scratches.

"Worgen." She spells it under her breath and gets it right the first time. "Zaranda's. Long way from Tethyr." She writes a short word after the name, possibly *work*. "The Fist takes men. Seatower, mornings, ask for the recruiting clerk. Don't come drunk, they'll keep you." The chalk taps once. "Beds. On the bridge they're cheap and damp. Inside the wall they're dearer and dry. The Basilisk Gate shuts late, but not *that* late."

Her board is crowded: tonight's names in neat columns, older ones half-smeared at the edges. Beside a handful of the faded names there's a small chalk cross, very carefully drawn. The newest one has been gone over twice.

Ilse sees where he's looking and turns the board a little toward herself. She doesn't make a show of it.

"Foot's free. Carts pay." Her eyes go to the card game beside the queue for a moment, then come back to him. "You'll want to keep walking, Worgen."

---

The cat answers him the way it always does: in pictures and feelings, not words.

*Man.* Between the two shuttered stalls, back against the planks, where the lamplight doesn't reach. *Still. Not hiding hard. Just still.* *Eyes on the barrel.* The card-man's hands moving, the cards going down, a drover's silver crossing the barrel. *Lips moving every time money moves.*

Then something closer, from right under the barrel: a sour, cold smell, like a cellar where the water never quite dries out, with a trace of old candle smoke. The cat's fur rises along its spine. *That. Don't like that.*

The cat stays at his heel with its tail fluffed and its eyes on the dark between the stalls. Behind him the queue shuffles forward. Ahead the bridge runs on under the lamps toward the walls of the Lower City.

"Late bell," Ilse says. She doesn't look up, and the drover behind James is already pushing up to the trestle.

James drifts out of the line and stops a little short of the barrel, at the edge of the small crowd. It's close enough to see the cards, and far enough back that nobody would take him for a player. The cat slips off his boot and drifts sideways along the planks like any bridge cat on its evening round.

Penhallow never stops talking. "There she is, friend, there's the lady, red as a bishop's blush. Watch her now, watch her go." A drover with a sunburnt neck puts down a silver. The cards move. For anyone who has dealt the throw a thousand times, there's nothing to it. Penhallow's right hand seems to drop its top card first, but it lets go of the bottom one. The queen stays pinched against his fingers for a heartbeat and goes down on the left, where the drover isn't looking. It's a good, clean hype, better than most on the southern coast. The drover points to the middle card and turns up a black jack. His silver goes into Penhallow's waistcoat pocket, and his friends laugh at him.

Next comes a boy, twelve or thirteen, all elbows, with the flat vowels of Elturel. He has a silver bit he holds like it's hot. This time Penhallow throws slowly, almost lazily. The queen goes exactly where any eye would follow it. The boy finds her. The crowd groans happily.

Penhallow doesn't pay the boy from the waistcoat pocket where the silver went. His left hand drops under the barrel's rim, and it comes back up with a fistful of coppers that he counts into the boy's palm: ten, along with the silver bit back. "Luck of the road, friend. Don't spend it all at once." The boy grins and is off north into the crowd before anyone can talk him into a second go.

Between the stalls, the still man's lips move.

Strong.* Wet stone, old wax, and underneath it something the cat has no picture for. Its fur rises at it. *Too strong.* It backs off, as he told it to.

Then it shows him one more thing on its way out: a single copper on the planks just inside the rim, where a coin might fall from a hand counting too fast. *Same smell. Smaller.*

The cat comes back to sit behind James's heel, facing the barrel, tail thick.

James keeps the boy's elbows in sight without shoving anyone. The cat flows along at his heel, keeping clear of boots.

At James's call the boy stops and turns, fast, with his back to a lamp-post and his right fist shut tight against his chest. Up close he's thinner than he looked at the barrel. One bootlace has snapped and been knotted twice, and the knot has come loose again. There's a fresh scrape across the knuckles of his free hand, still beaded, the sort you get from a fall onto planks.

He looks at James, then at the cloak, then down at the cat. The cat looks back at him, and its tail, which has been fluffed since the barrel, doesn't settle.

"Wren says I'm not to talk to men who follow me." The Elturel vowels are flat and careful. He doesn't run, though. His eyes go to the cat again. "...Is that yours?"

He shifts his weight. The fist stays shut.

"Four times. Maybe five." Pride creeps in over the wariness. "I've got the eye. He says so himself, says I'm the only one on the bridge who can follow his lady. Harl told me about the table, back when we came over. He said it was the easiest money on the whole crossing." His mouth closes on the name, and for a moment he looks younger than twelve. "Harl's... he's not about anymore."

Behind him a carter yells and the handcart's wheel squeals past. The boy flinches at the noise more than he should, then frowns at James.

I stop a few paces away, leaving him room to go.

"He's not about," he says again, flatly, as if that settles it.

Then the question reaches him, and he frowns. He's a boy deciding whether any of it counts as strange.

"No dreams." He shrugs. "Nobody asks about my coppers. Nobody'd *think* to, I'm not worth robbing." He lifts his left hand and shows the scraped knuckles like a joke on himself. "Just stupid stuff. I fell on the planks this morning, nothing there, I just went down. The lace went twice. A dog had me by the coat on Rivington steps yesterday, and it's never bothered anyone before." He hesitates. "Wren knocked the lamp over last night. That was her, not me. But it was my side of the room."

He frowns harder, as if he's only now hearing it all laid end to end.

"That's just luck, though, mister. Everybody has—"

"*Pim.*"

She comes through the crush the way people do when they've been searching for a while, quick and sideways, one shoulder first. She's maybe seventeen and wiry, with a sleeve rolled to the elbow and a gutting apron still tied on under a shawl. The smell of the fish stalls comes with her. Her hair is tied back hard, and she has the same flat vowels as the boy.

She doesn't shout at him. She steps in between, close, and moves Pim behind her with one hand on his chest, not roughly. Then she looks at James properly: the old cloak, the rod at his belt, the soft boots, the hands. Last of all she looks at the cat.

Through the bond, the cat gives him a brief impression of her: *fish, river, sweat, tired.* Then it adds, with something like relief: *Not that smell. Not on her.* Its tail is still thick, and its ears are on the fist behind her back.

"I heard you from the stalls." Wren keeps her voice down. It isn't a voice for a crowd. "Asking him about his coppers. And about Harl."

She doesn't let go of her brother.

"Harl came down from Elturel in the same cart as us. He started winning at that barrel in the summer. Then it was his laces, then his hand in a door, then a cart wheel over his foot. He laughed about it. Said a man that lucky at cards was bound to pay somewhere." Her jaw sets. "Then the river. And now Pim's got the eye, Dov says, and Pim's falling over nothing on dry planks."

Behind her, Pim says "*Wren*," embarrassed. She doesn't look round.

"So you tell me, James with the cat. What do *you* know about that table?"

I keep my voice low. “That’s what I know. I suspect the coins, but I can’t yet tell you what’s wrong with them or how to put it right.”

Wren listens to all of it without moving her hand off her brother's chest. When James says *separate bag*, her eyes narrow. When he says the cat reacts to Pim's winnings but not to her, she looks down at the cat, which is still staring at the boy's fist, tail still thick.

She doesn't answer about the sergeant. She looks at the scrap of cloth on his open palm, then at his face, and decides.

"Show him."

"Wren—"

"No bet, he said. Not buying. You heard him." She keeps her voice low and level. "Show him, Pim."

Pim's jaw works. He holds his shut fist up over the cloth for a long moment, like he's waiting for someone to grab it. Nobody does. Finally he turns his hand over and lets the coins slide out between his fingers without opening it all the way, and they land on the cloth in a little clatter. Ten coppers. The silver bit stays in his fist. He pulls his hand straight back against his chest.

The lamp on the post above them is good enough to see by. They're ordinary coppers at first glance: worn thin, mixed mints, one with a Tethyrian crown rubbed almost smooth, one clipped. Then James tips the cloth toward the light, and the edges catch it.

There's a mark on every one of them, on the rim and not the face, where nobody looks. It's tiny, smaller than a grain of rice: a branching shape pressed into the copper, not scratched, and dark, as if it had been burned in. A little antler.

He doesn't need a sage to tell him what it is. Every gambler on the southern coast knows that sign, and he has spent a lot of nights at tables with men who spat over their shoulder when someone said her name. Black antlers belong to Beshaba, the Maid of Misfortune, Tymora's sister and the other face of luck. He's seen the antler scratched on a loser's door, carved into a bandit's shield to frighten caravan guards, and drawn on the bottom of a bad dealer's cup as a joke. He has never seen it hidden on the rim of a coin, where only someone who knew to look would find it.

The coins are warm through the cloth, which is natural enough after the boy's fist. But the cloth is cool, and the warmth doesn't seem to be fading.

At his boot the cat has gone flat, with its ears back. Through the bond comes the same picture as at the barrel: *wet stone, old wax, the thing underneath.* Then, sharp: *On the cloth now. On you, close.* It doesn't come any nearer.

Wren has leaned in to look, and she sees the marks too. She doesn't know them, and James can tell from the way she squints. But she sees there are ten of them, one on every coin.

"That's on all of them." She straightens up. "Then he throws them in the river. Tonight."

"*No.*" Pim says it loud enough that a porter glances round. Then he drops his voice, but he doesn't back down. "I won them, Wren. Fair. That's two days' bread, mister. I've got the eye. They're *mine*."

Wren doesn't argue with him. She's looking at James.

"What's that on the edge?"

James opens the cloth on the trestle, below the lamp and out of sight of the queue. Ilse doesn't touch the coins either. She bends close, then closer, and finds the mark on the third coin. Once she's seen it, she finds it on the rest quickly.

"His barrel." It isn't a question. She looks at Pim and his bootlace, then at Wren. "Yours?"

"My brother," Wren says.

Ilse straightens up. She rolls the chalk once between her fingers, then puts it down.

She stops, and something comes back to her. "One of theirs came down here, though. Three weeks back, maybe four. A grey-haired priestess in the Hall's blue, with a little counting-board on a string. She stood by my queue half a morning asking people when they'd last made an offering to the Lady, and whether their prayers had been answered. Odd questions. Sister Aurenna, she called herself." Ilse's eyes go back to the coins. "I took her for a temple collecting money. Maybe she wasn't."

Behind them the queue is getting longer. Ilse looks past James at it, then at the hut.

"Ledgers are in there, if you want them. It's quiet enough now."

turns.reply:
The walk to the Rock takes them north against the evening traffic. They pass the shuttered stalls and the smell of the fish stalls. Coll is there now, leaning on a post with his arms folded, looking at a tray of eels as if he's thinking of buying one. Then the bridge widens and climbs. Wyrm's Rock rises out of the river in the middle of the crossing, black and wet at its foot. The fortress sits on top, and the roadway bends around its flank under the lamps.

Pim walks on the side away from the bundle, between his sister and the cat. He doesn't say anything. Twice his loose bootlace catches on a plank seam, and twice Wren takes hold of his collar before he can fall.

The chapel stair starts where the road bends: worn steps cut straight into the rock, climbing toward a door with a lamp above it. At the foot of the steps, set into the stone at about chest height, is the Lady's niche. It holds a weathered relief of a woman's face on a coin, worn smooth by hands, and in front of it a ledge of guttering candle-ends. There's an iron-bound box with a slot in the lid, chained to a ring in the rock.

Beside it an old man sits on an upturned crate behind a tray of tallow candles. He has a carter's hat and a carter's forearms, and a scarf wrapped twice around his throat against the damp coming off the river. He has already started counting the candles back into a basket.

The cat goes ahead of James for the first time since the barrel. It sniffs the bottom step and the base of the box. Through the bond comes a picture: *Wax. Honey-wax, old, lots. Hands. Copper.* A pause, and the fur along its back settles a little. *Not that smell. Clean.*

The old man looks up at the greeting and sees the worn coin in James's hand with the Lady's face on it. He looks at it longer than he looks at James.

"One of hers, are you? You don't look like a priest." He shifts on the crate with a grunt. "Aurenna. Aye. The grey sister. Sergeant Ilse sent you, did she?" He nods as if that makes sense of something. "Tobin Reeve. I mind the box. Sell the candles. Been doing it since my knees gave out for the reins."

He looks past James at Pim, then at Wren and her fish apron, and his voice drops a little.

"Boy in danger, you said." He doesn't ask which boy. "She was here a whole afternoon, the sister. Had me open the box for her. It's the Hall's box, she's got the right. She counted every coin in it with that little board of hers, click click click, and wrote it all down. Then she sat on that step and didn't say anything for a long while." He taps the iron lid with one knuckle. "She said the box ought to hold three times what it did. Said it's the same up and down the bridge, the same in Rivington. 'The tally's dead, Master Reeve.' That's what she said. Like a well gone dry. She asked me whether folk had stopped praying, or the Lady had stopped listening. I told her I sell candles, how would I know."

He scratches under the scarf.

"Tonight, though? You won't get to her tonight. She's up the hill behind the gates, and the Watch won't lift a bar for the likes of us." Then he holds up a finger, remembering. "But she's coming back. Said she'd count the box again on the twentieth, after the morning bell, and see if it was any better. The twentieth's tomorrow. She'll be here sometime after the bell. She's not one to be late, that one."

Pim has drifted to the candle ledge. He's looking at the guttering stubs, not at the old man, and his shut right hand is pressed against his coat. Tobin follows James's look.

"Copper a candle," he says, kindly enough. "Most folk light one for the road south. Some light one for somebody who's not coming back up it." He goes on packing the basket. "I'm off when the last lamp's lit. My knees won't take the river damp past that."

He doesn't say anything.

Wren looks at the cord, then at the old man. "Thanks." She threads it through the eyelets with quick fish-stall fingers and pulls it tight. Pim stands still and lets her.

She stays crouched a moment longer before she answers.

"We've half a room in Rivington, over Dunmore's cooperage by the steps. A widow and her two have the other half. It's dry, and the door has a bar." She stands up and wipes her hands on her apron. "Safe, I don't know anymore. He fell over on dry planks."

Her eyes go to the bundle in James's hand.

Tobin lifts a hand from his basket. "Aye. Mind the boy on them steps. They're slick after dark." He hoists the basket onto his hip with a grunt, says something under his breath about his knees, and starts up the road toward the north end without looking back. The two candles stay burning on the ledge behind them.

Wren listens to all of it standing still. She looks at Pim, then at the cloth bundle, then back at James.

"Not ours, then." She sounds like a girl crossing one worry off a list. "Good. The widow's two would wake at a cat anyway."

They walk south, back the way they came. The bridge is thinner now that the lamps are lit and the carts have mostly gone through. Coll is still at the fish stalls, still looking at the same tray of eels, which have been put away under a wet sack. Dov is still at his barrel with two new drovers. He doesn't look up this time, and his patter doesn't change. The space between the shuttered stalls is empty.

Pim walks with his new lace slapping nowhere. It holds. Twice he looks down at it as if he expects it to go.

Halfway to the steps Wren speaks again, low, without turning her head.

"Beds I'll take. For him. Not for nothing, though." Her eyes stay on the planks ahead. "I gut fish across from that barrel twelve hours a day. I see what goes on there. Once a week Dov goes down the Rivington steps early, before the boats come in. His bag's flat when he goes and fat when he comes back. Last time was market day. Tomorrow's market day." She glances at James. "That's what I pay with. You want more, ask me what I've seen. I'll tell you true."

At the top of the steps a woman stands behind a hatch in a wall, stout and floury to the elbows, with a tray of pies under a cloth and a brazier glowing beside her. The smell of mutton and pepper reaches them in the cold.

"There's the Stave and Hoop at the bottom, by Dunmore's yard," Wren says. "Carters use it. It has a fire in the common room and the keeper's a woman. A silver a bed in the long room, five for a room with a door. She knows me. She won't cheat you."

“That’s useful, Wren. Thank you. Tomorrow I’d like to hear exactly which way he goes.”

turns.reply:
"Three, love." The pie-woman takes his six coppers with floury fingers and drops them into a tin without counting them. She lifts the pies out with a wooden paddle and wraps each one in a twist of brown paper. The paper goes dark with grease at once.

Pim takes his in both hands. For the first time since the barrel, his right fist opens. Wren looks at the pie James holds out to her, then at his face. She takes it.

"Two pies, then," she says, as if writing it on a slate. She bites into hers before she says anything else, like someone who hasn't eaten since noon.

At *which way he goes* she chews, swallows and shakes her head.

"I see him go *down*. From the stalls that's all you see, the top of the steps and his back. The bottom's round the bend, behind Dunmore's roof." She licks pepper off her thumb. "Before the boats, I said. The first boats are tied up by the morning bell. So earlier than that. I'm setting out trays by then, I can't leave them." She looks at James sideways. "You'd have to be at the bottom already."

---

The Rivington steps are worn hollow in the middle and wet from the river mist. Lamps hang from brackets on the house walls, one every few turns, and between them the stone shines black. Wren goes first with her shawl pulled tight. Pim goes in the middle, eating with his whole attention. James takes the outside edge, and the folded cloth rides in his left hand, away from the boy.

Halfway down, Pim's new lace holds and his foot holds too. His pie doesn't. A bite of crust breaks off, the whole thing tips in its paper, and the bottom half drops out onto the step and rolls down three more, leaving a trail of gravy.

Pim stares after it. "...That was *mine*."

"It was," says Wren. She breaks her own pie in two without stopping and pushes the bigger half into his hand.

---

The cat drops back on the turns. It sits on a step above them, looks up the way they came, then runs down to catch up. It does this three times. Through the bond come pictures, plain and unbothered:

*Woman with a basket, going up. Not us.* A man with a lantern on a pole stops at a door, knocks, goes in. *Gone.* Two carters coming down behind them, loud, smelling of beer, and they turn off at the first lane. *Not us.* The cat looks up the empty steps one last time, all the way to the brazier glowing at the hatch. *Nobody. Nobody keeps.*

Then it gives him one more thing, very pleased: *Pie. On the step. Mine?*

---

The bottom of the steps opens onto a lane of packed earth along the river, with a smell of tar, shavings and woodsmoke. On the right is Dunmore's cooperage, a big shed with its doors barred and staves stacked under the eaves, and a lit window above it with a rag across half the glass. Wren glances up at it and walks on.

The Stave and Hoop stands next door. It's low and wide, with a barrel-hoop nailed over the door for a sign and the shape of firelight moving behind horn panes. Inside, the common room is warm enough that James's face prickles. There are two long tables, a dozen carters at their bowls and a fire built high in a broad hearth. There's a dog asleep in front of it too. It lifts its head at the cat, decides it isn't worth the trouble and puts it down again.

The keeper comes out from behind the trestle wiping her hands. She's a broad woman of fifty with a man's leather apron and her sleeves pinned up. She looks at Wren first.

"Wren, girl. Not your night for it, is it." Then she looks at Pim with gravy on his chin, then at James, the old cloak and the cat, and last at the little cloth bundle he holds away from his body. "And company."

"He's paying," Wren says. "Beds. For tonight."

The keeper nods as if that's the most ordinary thing in the world. "Hessa Tull. I keep the place." She says it to James. "Cat's welcome, it can have my mice. Long room's a silver a head, straw's fresh this week. A room with a door is five, and there's one left at the top, over the kitchen, warm." She waits a moment. "Which is it, and how many?"

---

James scrapes the last of the barley from the bowl and puts the spoon down. Then he leans toward the folded cloth on the bench without opening it. He knows Beshaba's antler from the tables. What it *does* is another matter, and he goes looking for the answer in everything he has heard over the years: temple teaching, the Lady's own lore, and the long nights when old players talked about cursed stakes.

It comes back to him in pieces, some from the temple and more from the tables.

There's the Lady's own teaching first. Her sister's gifts are never really given away. They're *placed*, and they stay where they were placed until someone moves them properly. Then there are the old players' stories, which say the same thing more crudely. James heard one in a Zazesspur gambling-den from a man missing three fingers. He told of a Calishite who won a cursed stake and threw it off a pier the same night, and he drowned off that pier a month later. *You can't drop it in a ditch,* the man had said. *It goes with the winning, not with the coin.* The curse follows whoever the coin belongs to, by the way it came to them: won, paid or given. It doesn't follow whoever happens to be holding it.

James can work the rest out for himself, and none of it is good. The ten coppers in the cloth are Pim's by winning. James only carries them, and in every version of the story he knows, a thing carried for someone else still belongs to that person. Wrapping them keeps them off the boy's skin and nothing more. Throwing them in the river, as Wren wanted, probably wouldn't help either.

His second question is answered by the same tales. A cursed stake handed to someone who doesn't know what it is takes its weight with it to them. That's the whole point of a stake like that. If Pim gave the ten coppers to someone else, or spent them on bread, or paid a debt with them, the misfortune would go with the coins. The baker or the widow next door would carry it then. The stories also tell of a cleaner way: the curse goes back the way it came, across the same table and by the same kind of bargain, to whoever put it there. What happens to that person afterwards, the stories never agree on. Not one of them mentions a mark pressed into the rim, or a dealer who pays out from a separate bag.

---

The bundle is still on the bench where all three of them can see it. Bed is waiting, and so is the late bell, whenever you want either.

It's only a few yards along the lane to Dunmore's. Sentry goes first, low against the stacked staves. A side stair runs up the outside of the shed, steep and slick with river damp. Wren takes it with one hand on the rail and the other behind her for Pim's sleeve. At the top she knocks twice, waits, and knocks once more.

The bar scrapes. The woman who opens the door is about forty and narrow-faced, with a shawl over her nightdress and a rushlight in a dish. Behind her, the room has been split down the middle by a blanket hung on a cord. On her side two small shapes are asleep in one bed, one of them snoring like an old man.

She looks past Wren at James, at his cloak and at the cat on the step, and her face shuts.

"He's paying our beds at Hessa's tonight," Wren says before the woman can ask. "We're fetching a thing. Two breaths, Nell."

Nell Garrow looks at James a moment longer. Then she stands aside without a word and takes her rushlight back to her mending. She doesn't look up again. It's a woman's habit when the business is none of hers and she'd like it to stay that way.

Sentry won't come over the threshold. It sits on the top step with its tail wrapped round its feet, and through the bond it sends him a feeling first: *in there. Same.* After a moment it sends something stronger and more precise: *Floor. By the wall. More than the cloth.*

Wren goes straight to the wall on their side of the blanket, kneels, and works a knife-tip under a short board. It comes up without a sound, as if it has done this often. Under it is a grey wool stocking knotted at the top. She lifts it out by the knot and doesn't open it. Then, under James's eyes, she does open it, just enough to tip a few coins into the rushlight on her palm.

The mark is on the rim of every one. They're the same little dark antlers.

She pours the coins back and counts the rest by touch through the wool, her lips moving. She stops and frowns.

"Thirty." She looks at Pim. "Four lots. That's forty."

Pim has gone red to the ears again. He keeps his voice down, for the sleeping children.

"First lot went through my coat. There was a hole in the pocket, I didn't know. On the bridge, by the Rock." He shoves his hand into the pocket and shows them his fingers poking out the bottom; nobody has mended it. "I thought that was the bad luck. Losing it straight off. Before you started keeping them."

Wren closes her eyes for half a breath. Then she knots the stocking shut, puts the board back, and stands up.

"Same as the river, then," she says to James, low. It isn't a question. Then she says to her brother, not unkindly, "Hole gets sewn tomorrow."

She goes out past Nell's mending with the stocking held away from her body, as James held the bundle.

---

Going down the stair, Pim keeps hold of the rail with both hands.

At the bottom Wren stops in the lane and answers what James said by the fire. She has clearly turned it over on the way.

"Ilse." She says the name like a price she doesn't like. "You tell her the silver and the coppers. She'll hear it from you. From a fish-girl she'd hear it and forget it." She shifts the stocking to her other hand. "If she asks me is it true, I'll say yes. To her face. That much I'll do."

The window of the Stave and Hoop glows a few yards on. Sentry trots ahead to the door and waits there, looking back at the stocking.

*Two lots now,* it tells him. *Both on the boy.* Its tail stays thick until they're inside.

The bar won't go across for a while yet. The fire's still up, and you can do what you like with the rest of the evening.

Pim's eyes go back toward the dark lane and the bridge above it. They stay there a moment too long before he answers.

The room at the top is small and close, warm from the kitchen chimney running up one wall. It has a narrow bed with a blanket folded at its foot, one shelf over the bed, one by the door and a horn window gone yellow with smoke. Sentry comes up the stair behind them and stops on the top step, the same as at Dunmore's. It sits there with its tail around its feet and doesn't cross.

Wren sets the stocking on the shelf by the door, knot facing out. James puts the folded cloth beside it. Pim watches every inch of it with his arms crossed tight over his coat.

At *forty here, ten lost, none spent*, Pim counts with his lips moving: the stocking, the cloth, then the hole in his pocket, which he touches through the coat.

"Forty. Ten lost." He nods once. "None spent. That's right, mister."

Wren is already turning the blanket down. "Third bed from the door," she says, not looking round. "I heard."

---

The long room is dark and smells of fresh straw and carters' boots. The third bed doesn't creak, as Hessa promised. James lies down with his pack against the wall and the rod within reach. Sentry walks the length of the room once, inspects every snoring carter, and settles against the backs of his knees.

Somewhere out over the river the late bell rings. A little later Hessa's bar goes across the door with a heavy wooden knock. The dog by the hearth sighs at it.

Some hours into the dark a thump comes through the ceiling at the kitchen end of the house. Something has fallen up there, not hard, but it isn't nothing. A low voice follows, Wren's, and then nothing more. Nobody comes down the stair.

Sentry's head is up. Through the bond: *Up. The boy's room. Something fell.* A pause while it listens. *Girl awake. Quiet now.* Its head goes back down, but one ear stays turned toward the stair until James stops feeling it.

note.text:
The strongest part was how naturally the investigation grew out of arriving in the city. I had no quest, but the cards tempted James, the cat noticed something wrong, and Ilse gave me enough reason to get involved without hiring me. That felt well matched to this character.

**What worked**
- Wren and Pim felt like people rather than information dispensers. Pim’s pride in “having the eye,” his insistence on keeping his own coins, and Wren negotiating how she could repay help made the stakes personal.
- Sentry was excellent: useful sensory impressions, clear limits, and enough personality that naming the cat became a genuinely enjoyable moment.
- The clues developed coherently: separate payout bag, marked rims, selective victims, earlier winnings, then Dov’s morning supply trip. My questions and decisions seemed to uncover the story rather than merely advance a script.
- The Religion check was worthwhile. Its answer changed what I could responsibly do with the coins. Not rolling for straightforward conversations also kept play moving.

**What broke or dragged**
- Too many responses restated my entire turn, sometimes nearly line for line, before supplying the next development. That slowed otherwise good scenes.
- The repeated out-of-game explanations that honest conversation needed no roll were unnecessary. Just resolving those actions was enough.
- Timekeeping became inconsistent. Around quarter past nine, the late bell was still ahead; after further activity, I somehow completed eight hours’ rest before the first boats and morning bell. The schedule mattered because I was planning to intercept Dov.
- A “debt” for Wren’s pies appeared despite my offering supper freely. Wren can certainly *feel* indebted, but the journal should distinguish her intention from an obligation James accepted.

**What was missing**
- A little more actionable geography and timing: how long to reach the bridge from the inn, roughly when Dov usually passes, and how that relates to Aurenna’s arrival.
- More pressure or change outside our conversations. Coll watching Dov was promising, but much of the evening became a sequence of discussions and arrangements. One concrete update from that surveillance could have kept the wider world present.
- A clearer opportunity to respond to the nighttime thump. It was narrated inside the sleep-to-morning transition, which made a potentially important danger feel unavailable for intervention.

Overall, I cared about keeping these two safe, enjoyed playing James’s restraint around cards, and finished with a plan I wanted to pursue. Keep the characterful dialogue and clue logic; trim repetition and make the clock dependable.

after.text:
Yes—the thump from Pim and Wren’s room during the night. I wanted to get up, knock quietly, and check that neither of them was hurt. We already knew Pim’s misfortune was escalating, so “something fell” wasn’t a sound James would comfortably ignore.

But that event and Hessa waking me in the morning arrived in the same response. By the time I could act, the night had passed and the long rest was complete. I felt I’d missed the chance rather than chosen to stay in bed.

Stopping at Sentry’s warning would have given me a meaningful decision: investigate and risk interrupting my rest, or trust Wren to handle it.

opening.text:
The Trade Way ends in noise. Carts grind onto the stones of Wyrm's Crossing, porters shout over each other, and somewhere above the river a bell marks the evening. Lamps are being lit one by one along the bridge. Houses and shopfronts lean over the span, so the crossing feels less like a road and more like a narrow, crowded street hanging over the Chionthar.

The queue at the checkpoint shuffles forward. A family with bundles on their backs passes the trestle table; a carter argues about a toll and loses. Behind the table, a Flaming Fist sergeant with ink on her fingers and a chipped red gauntlet rubs her eyes and writes on a chalkboard without looking up much.

A few paces off the line, a lean man in a too-good waistcoat has turned a barrel into a table. Three cards flick under his hands, face down, face up, face down. "Find the lady, friends, find the lady! Long road, short game, a silver says you've still got your eye!" A couple of waiting drovers lean in to watch. The cards slap down again, crisp and familiar.

At James's feet, the cat has stopped. Its tail is up and its ears are turned, not toward the cards, but somewhere along the bridge, where the lamplight thins between two shuttered stalls.

The man in front of James steps up to the table. The sergeant's chalk taps the board.

"Next after this one — name, and your business in the Gate."
